lesson.title: What You're Allowed, and Wise, to Call a Variable
lesson.summary: Python enforces strict, specific rules about which names are legal for variables, and separately from those rules, following shared naming conventions makes code far easier for other people, and your future self, to read.
lesson.body:
The name you choose on the left side of an assignment statement is not entirely free. Python enforces a fixed set of rules for what counts as a legal identifier, the technical term for a name used for a variable, function, or similar item. A legal name must start with a letter, upper or lower case, or an underscore character, and after that first character, it may contain any combination of letters, digits, and underscores. A name cannot start with a digit, cannot contain spaces, and cannot contain most punctuation or symbols such as a hyphen or an at sign. Python is also case-sensitive, which means score and Score are treated as two completely different names, not the same name written differently.

There is one more restriction: a name cannot be one of Python's reserved keywords, a fixed list of words the language itself uses for its own syntax, including words like if, for, while, def, class, True, False, None, and import. These words are reserved because Python's interpreter relies on recognizing them to understand the structure of your code, so allowing them to also be used as variable names would make code impossible to parse correctly.

Some examples make the boundary between legal and illegal clear:

total_score = 100      # legal
_hidden = True          # legal, may start with an underscore
score2 = 50             # legal, digits are fine after the first character

Compare those to attempts that break the rules, which Python will reject with a SyntaxError before the program even runs: a name like 2nd_score is illegal because it starts with a digit rather than a letter or underscore. A name like my score, written with a space in the middle, is illegal because Python would read it as two separate names sitting next to each other rather than one identifier. Writing class = "Math" is illegal for a different reason entirely, not because of characters or spacing, but because class is a reserved keyword that Python needs for defining classes, so it cannot also serve as a variable name.

Beyond what Python strictly requires, there are also widely shared conventions that are not enforced by the interpreter at all but are followed by nearly every Python programmer, documented in a style guide called PEP 8. The most common convention is snake_case, writing multiword variable names in all lowercase with underscores between words, such as total_score rather than totalScore or TotalScore. Choosing descriptive names, such as total_score instead of a vague name like ts or x, costs nothing at runtime but makes a real difference to anyone reading the code later, including the person who wrote it. Just as comments add information for human readers without changing what the interpreter does, thoughtful naming is a second, quieter way of making code communicate clearly, on top of simply obeying the rules that keep it from crashing outright.
